findings.message: The explicit `size="xxs"` prop (which mapped to font-size 16x) was dropped when switching from `<Icon name={icon} size="xxs" />` to `<GlobalIconWrapper icon={icon} className={styles.icon} />`. For string icons, GlobalIconWrapper now calls `<Icon name={icon} className={styles.icon} />`, which defaults to `size="md"` (22x). The Badge's `.icon { font-size: var(--base-sizing-16x) }` class and Icon's `.md { font-size: var(--base-sizing-22x) }` class are both applied to the same span with equal CSS specificity (single class each), making the rendered size non-deterministic and dependent on stylesheet injection order.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: old code used `size="xxs"` (Icon's own 16x CSS class). New code passes `className={styles.icon}` (Badge's 16x class) while Icon defaults to `size="md"` (22x class). Both single-class selectors land on the same span element. CSS specificity is equal, so the winner depends on stylesheet injection order — a fragile, non-deterministic result.
findings.severity_justification: Icon size in Badge may render at 22x instead of the intended 16x depending on stylesheet injection order — a visual regression that could affect production. Not data-loss or functional, but a real user-facing inconsistency.
findings.category_justification: Dropping the explicit `size` prop in favor of a competing CSS class introduces a visual rendering inconsistency — the icon may not display at the intended size.

findings.message: The explicit `size="lg"` prop (24x) was dropped when switching from `<Icon size="lg" name={icon} />` to `<GlobalIconWrapper icon={icon} className={styles.icon} />`. For string icons, GlobalIconWrapper now calls `<Icon name={icon} className={styles.icon} />` with the default `size="md"` (22x). The Accordion's `.icon { font-size: var(--base-sizing-24x) }` and Icon's `.md { font-size: var(--base-sizing-22x) }` apply to the same span with equal CSS specificity, creating a non-deterministic size conflict (22x vs 24x).
findings.tp_fp_justification: The Accordion's `.icon` rule is nested inside `.Root` in the SCSS, compiling to `.Root .icon` (specificity 0,2,0), which is higher than Icon's flat `.md` class (specificity 0,1,0). The descendant selector reliably wins, rendering the icon at 24x — same as the old `size="lg"`. The finding's claim of equal specificity is factually incorrect.
findings.severity_justification: The concern is moot because nesting ensures deterministic specificity; no actual size conflict exists.
findings.category_justification: The finding concerns CSS specificity and rendered icon size.

findings.message: `iconProps` is defined in the interface and forwarded to `Icon` only for string icons, but is silently ignored when `icon` is a ReactElement. There's no error or warning, so callers who pass `iconProps` with a ReactElement will see their configuration silently dropped. Given that none of the five consuming components actually pass `iconProps`, this prop has no real usage, making it dead API surface that creates a misleading contract.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: `iconProps` is declared in `GlobalIconWrapperProps` and forwarded to `<Icon>` only for string icons, silently ignored for ReactElement. A grep confirms no consumer passes `iconProps` — it is unused API surface. The asymmetric behavior without any warning creates a misleading contract.
findings.severity_justification: No current caller is affected since `iconProps` has zero usages. The risk is future misuse by a caller who passes `iconProps` with a ReactElement and is silently ignored, but this is a minor API quality issue rather than a functional bug.
findings.category_justification: The issue is about an exported interface prop that creates a misleading contract — callers cannot rely on `iconProps` working regardless of icon type, and the prop has no real usage, making it dead API surface.

findings.message: The ReactElement wrapper span uses hardcoded inline styles (`style={{ display: "inline-flex", alignItems: "center" }}`) instead of a CSS module. The prior art in this codebase (the existing GlobalIconWrapper on origin/main at `Motif/GlobalIconWrapper/GlobalIconWrapper.tsx`) uses a CSS module with a `.Root` class that also includes `> :not(svg) { font-size: 1em }`. This rule ensures non-SVG icon children (e.g., `<i>` tags used by icon libraries like Font Awesome) inherit the correct em-based font-size from the parent. The new implementation omits this rule, so `<i>`-based custom icons will not scale correctly with the component's font-size.
findings.tp_fp_justification: The checked-out GlobalIconWrapper uses inline styles without `> :not(svg) { font-size: 1em }`. This rule (present in the PR diff's CSS module version) defensively overrides any fixed font-size from icon library CSS. Without it, icon libraries that set their own fixed font-size on `<i>` elements won't scale with the container. The factual claim about the missing rule is correct, though the 'prior art on origin/main' framing is wrong — that CSS module version was created within this PR and then refactored away.
findings.severity_justification: Affects only icon libraries that set a fixed font-size on their icon elements; common libraries like Bootstrap Icons and Material Symbols rely on inheritance and work fine without it. Narrow real-world impact.
findings.category_justification: Missing CSS rule that could cause incorrect icon scaling for certain external icon libraries.

findings.message: Two separate `render()` calls are made within the same test without calling `cleanup()` between them. Both accordion components remain mounted in the document for the rest of the test. The Avatar test in the same PR correctly uses `rerender` for testing the second icon variant. The inconsistency aside, if a future change adds 'home' text to the second render, `getByText('home')` will throw due to multiple matches. Should use `const { rerender } = render(...)` then `rerender(...)` to stay consistent and avoid DOM accumulation.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: Accordion test uses two separate `render()` calls in the same test at the SHA, accumulating both components in the DOM simultaneously. Avatar test (same PR) correctly uses `rerender`. The inconsistency is real and the DOM accumulation is confirmed, even if no current assertion fails.

findings.category_justification: The issue is about test structure: multiple render calls without cleanup, DOM accumulation, and inconsistency with the rerender pattern used elsewhere in the same PR.

findings.message: `GlobalIconWrapper` is called without a `className` here, making Avatar the only component that doesn't pass one. For string icons this falls through to `<Icon name={icon} />` with no wrapping class; sizing is controlled by the Avatar CSS descendant rule `&.icon span { font-size }`. However, for ReactElement icons the wrapper span has no class at all, so all styling depends on the ancestor `.icon span` selector continuing to match. If the Avatar's HTML structure changes (e.g., an extra wrapper element is added), icon sizing silently breaks. Passing `className` makes the sizing intent explicit and resilient, consistent with all other uses of GlobalIconWrapper in this PR.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: Avatar calls `<GlobalIconWrapper icon={icon} />` without className — the only component that omits it. Icon sizing depends entirely on the `.md.icon span` descendant selector in Avatar.module.scss. For ReactElement icons, the wrapper span has no class. Adding any intermediate wrapper element would silently break icon sizing. The inconsistency with all other GlobalIconWrapper usages is confirmed.
findings.severity_justification: Current behavior is correct — sizing works via the descendant selector. The concern is structural fragility if the DOM layout changes, not a current defect. Minor maintainability risk.
findings.category_justification: The issue is structural fragility and inconsistency with sibling components — Avatar relies on a CSS descendant selector for icon sizing rather than a direct class, making it brittle to future DOM structure changes.

findings.message: `GlobalIconWrapper` (and `MotifIcon` in the else branch) are rendered as direct children of `<ul>` without being wrapped in a `<li>`. This is invalid HTML — the only permitted direct children of `<ul>` are `<li>`, `<script>`, and `<template>`. While browsers tolerate this, it is an accessibility concern: screen readers following the list role expect only `<li>` children, and the icon is invisible to the list's accessible structure. A `<li aria-hidden="true">` wrapper is the minimal fix.
findings.tp_fp_justification: Verified: GlobalIconWrapper and MotifIcon are both rendered as direct <ul> children without <li> wrappers in the checked-out code. This is invalid HTML and an accessibility concern. However, this pattern pre-dates the PR — the old <Icon> component also rendered a <span> directly in <ul>. The PR only replaced the icon implementation, not the structural issue.
findings.severity_justification: Invalid HTML in a navigation component with accessibility implications — screen readers relying on list structure may not correctly interpret the breadcrumb. Real concern for a11y compliance, though browsers tolerate it.
findings.category_justification: Direct <span> children of <ul> is both invalid HTML and an accessibility issue for the breadcrumb navigation's list structure as interpreted by screen readers.

Any change to either component's wrapper structure would silently misfire. This is a concrete fragility in the specific test code.

findings.message: The GlobalIconWrapper component does not validate or sanitize the non-string input for the 'icon' prop. A malicious React element could execute unintended behavior when inserted into the DOM, creating a potential security risk.
findings.tp_fp_justification: React's JSX rendering is inherently safe from script injection — rendering `{icon}` goes through React's virtual DOM, not innerHTML. A 'malicious ReactElement' requires controlling source code, meaning code execution is already compromised. No concrete exploitation path, no untrusted input flow, and no use of dangerouslySetInnerHTML. This is a generic boilerplate security concern not grounded in the actual code.
findings.severity_justification: No actual vulnerability exists — React's rendering model prevents the claimed risk by design.
findings.category_justification: The finding is framed as a security risk around unsanitized ReactElement rendering.

findings.message: The use of GlobalIconWrapper assumes that either 'icon' is a valid string for the Icon component or a valid React element. No fallback or validation exists for unexpected values, which could break the UI.

GlobalIconWrapper's `typeof icon === 'string'` covers both valid cases. The finding is generic boilerplate with no specific unexpected value identified, no concrete UI break demonstrated, and no account of the existing type constraints.
findings.severity_justification: No concrete failure mode exists — TypeScript types constrain valid inputs and the existing guards handle edge cases.
findings.category_justification: The finding is framed as a runtime correctness concern about missing input validation.
